title: Group B: Midland Metro Transit
text:
Your Organization
Midland Metro Transit is the public bus authority serving a mid-sized Midwestern city of about 180,000 people. It operates 22 routes, runs roughly 6 AM to midnight, and carries about 14,000 riders on a typical weekday. The agency has 340 employees: 210 bus operators, 40 mechanics and maintenance staff, dispatchers, planners, customer service staff, and an administrative and leadership team.
Transit is a public agency — it’s funded by a combination of fare revenue (about 20% of its budget), city and county subsidies, and state and federal grants. The board of directors is appointed by elected officials. Decisions about routes, fares, and service levels are technically made by the board, but in practice they emerge from a messy mix of staff recommendations, public comment, political pressure, and budget constraints.
Bus operators are the face of the agency. They interact with hundreds of passengers a day — handling fares, answering questions, managing conflicts, and making decisions about safety. They’re also the people most likely to know what’s actually happening on the ground: which stops are dangerous at night, which routes are always overcrowded, where the potholes are. But they work largely alone, they are busy, and their feedback reaches management through a long chain.
The agency has been struggling. Ridership dropped sharply during COVID and hasn’t fully recovered. The agency is facing a budget shortfall, pressure from the city to expand service to underserved neighborhoods, and a tight labor market that’s made hiring drivers difficult. Meanwhile, an ongoing contract negotiation with the drivers’ union has stalled.

Work through the discussion questions with your group.

title: Case Study: Culture Clash at Meridian-Apex
text:
Background
Meridian Analytics is a 12-year-old data consulting firm known for its rigorous processes, formal hierarchy, and conservative culture. Dress code is business professional. Meetings start and end exactly on time. Decisions go through a clear chain of approval. The firm’s motto, displayed in the lobby, is “Precision. Reliability. Trust.” Turnover is low; many employees have been there for a decade or more. Clients are mostly Fortune 500 companies and government agencies.
Apex Labs is a 4-year-old product analytics startup that Meridian just acquired. Apex has 30 employees, no dress code, an open floor plan with a ping-pong table, and a culture of fast iteration and public disagreement. Decisions are made in Slack threads, often without managers involved. Their internal motto is “Ship it, then fix it.” Turnover is high but accepted — people come in intense, contribute, and move on. Clients are mostly early-stage tech companies.
Meridian’s leadership announced the acquisition as a way to “bring Apex’s innovation energy into Meridian’s trusted infrastructure.” They plan to integrate the two teams within six months.

title: Case Study: Culture Clash at Meridian-Apex
text:
Part 1: Culture Mapping
Using Schein’s three levels of organizational culture, map each organization:








Level
Meridian Analytics
Apex Labs




Artifacts (visible: physical space, rituals, language, dress, symbols)




Espoused values (what the org says it believes)




Basic assumptions (what the org actually believes, often unstated)





Complete the table together before moving to Part 2.

title: Case Study: Culture Clash at Meridian-Apex
text:
Part 2: Systems Thinking
The merger creates a new combined system. Using systems theory concepts from Ch. 4:

Interdependence: Identify two or three places where Meridian and Apex are now interdependent in ways they weren’t before. What happens in one part of the system that will now affect the other?
Feedback loops: What feedback mechanisms exist (or should exist) to help leadership know whether the integration is working? What signals might they miss?
Equifinality: The goal is a successfully integrated organization. What are two or three different ways the combined company could reach that goal? What does this suggest about how Meridian’s leadership should approach the merger?

title: Case Study: Culture Clash at Meridian-Apex
text:
Part 3: Communication Diagnosis

Meridian’s CEO sent a company-wide email on day one of the acquisition that said: “We are thrilled to welcome the Apex team. Their innovative spirit will strengthen everything we do. Business as usual for now — more details to come.”
What does this message communicate about assumptions, values, and power — beyond what it literally says? How might Apex employees read it differently than Meridian employees?
If you were advising the integration team, what is the single most important communication act they should take in the first 30 days, and why?

title: Group A: KAPOW (Kokomo Auto Parts & Outfitting Works)
text:
Your Organization
KAPOW (Kokomo Auto Parts & Outfitting Works) is a metal stamping plant in Kokomo, Indiana that manufactures structural components for pickup trucks and SUVs. Founded in 1962, it employs 380 people across three shifts — about 290 on the production floor and 90 in supervisory, engineering, quality, HR, logistics, and administrative roles. The workforce is unionized and has been for 40 years.
The plant runs around the clock to meet just-in-time delivery contracts with two major automakers. A missed delivery is a huge deal for the company and can shut down an assembly line 200 miles away. Quality defects caught downstream can trigger expensive recalls and damage the relationship. The margin for error is thin.
On the floor, work is organized around production cells. Each cell has a team leader (not quite a supervisor, but the first point of contact for problems). Supervisors oversee multiple cells on a shift. Above them are department managers, a plant manager, and corporate liaisons from the parent company — a mid-size Ohio manufacturer that acquired KAPOW in 2019.
The workforce skews older — average tenure is 14 years. A significant share of employees are first- or second-generation immigrants from Mexico and Central America; Spanish is widely spoken on two of the three shifts. The union contract governs everything from break schedules to grievance procedures, and the union steward is often the first person workers turn to when something goes wrong.

Work through the discussion questions with your group.

title: Theory Application Short Paper
text: The goal of this assignment is to apply a theoretical lens to a real organizational situation. Ideally, you will be able to use the theory to gain new insights into the situation, and will see something you wouldn’t have noticed otherwise.

title: Theory Application Short Paper
text:
What to do
1. Choose a concept. Pick one specific concept or theory from any chapter we’ve covered so far.
2. Find an example. Identify a real-world situation that your concept can help explain. This can be something from your own experience in an organization or a current or recent event you’ve read about. Describe the situation briefly.
3. Apply the theory. Explain the concept in your own words and show how your example illustrates it. What does viewing the situation through the lens of the concept / framework reveal that you wouldn’t otherwise see? Are there limitations to the theory? Are there aspects of this situation that remain unexplained or confusing?
4. Conclusion. Reflect broadly on the broader implications of your analysis: what it reveals about organizations and communication?

Length: 2–3 pages, double-spaced
Format: 12-point font, 1-inch margins. Cite the textbook (or any other course reading) if you quote or paraphrase it. You do not need a formal reference list for a brief citation, but do include enough information for me to find the source (author, chapter, page number).
Submit: Brightspace by Monday, Oct 26

title: Final Paper: Organizational Communication Analysis
text: For this assignment you will apply what you have learned in this class toward understanding a real organization that you are familiar with.

title: Final Paper: Organizational Communication Analysis
text:
Suggested structure
Introduction (~1 page). Introduce the organization and your relationship to it. State your analytical focus: what communication dynamic or challenge you’ll examine, and which frameworks you’ll bring to it, and why this is the correct lens for understanding it. Your goal is to argue that these frameworks illuminate something important about the organization, and that your analysis will reveal something that wasn’t obvious before.
Analysis (~3–4 pages). Apply at least two theoretical frameworks from the course. For each one, clearly introduce the dynamic or challenge you’ll be examining, and show how this framework helps to understand it in a new way. Use concrete evidence from your experience in the organization to outline what is happening: things you witnessed, conversations you had, policies you encountered, patterns you noticed. Then, analyze the evidence through the lens of the framework. What does it tell us about the organization? What does it reveal, and what might it predict about the future of the organization or its processes?
Conclusion (~1 page). Do some bigger picture thinking to answer questions like: What are some of the broader implications of your analysis? What are some limitations of your analysis? What would you recommend to someone in a leadership role there, or what does the analysis explain that you previously couldn’t account for?

title: Final Paper: Organizational Communication Analysis
text:
In-class presentation
Your presentation (Dec 8 or 10) is a condensed version of this same analysis. You will probably use slides, but you are welcome to propose something more creative. The presentation should be no more than 5 minutes long, and should include the following:

Briefly introduce the organization and your relationship to it
Explain how at least one framework illuminates something important about the organization
Talk about a takeaway from your analysis that you think is important for the class to understand


Length: 5–7 pages, double-spaced (not counting references)
Sources: Cite the textbook and at least one other additional reading. Use any consistent citation format (APA, MLA, Chicago).
Submit: Paper on Brightspace by Monday, Dec 7. Presentations in class Dec 8 and Dec 10.

title: What is an Organization? Activities
text:
I’ll write each group name around the room. You will go around with a marker and mark whether you think each group is an organization or not.
Discussion prompt after the walk: What features seemed to matter most in deciding? What kept coming up?




Group A: Apple Inc. 160,000 employees worldwide. Formal hierarchy, explicit goals, legal incorporation, products you can buy. Is it an organization?

Group B: Your Family Five people who live together, share finances, have meals together, and have unspoken roles (who does dishes, who picks up kids). Is it an organization?

Group C: The Purdue Student Body 50,000 students enrolled at Purdue. They all pay tuition, share a campus, and are governed by the same university rules — but most have never met each other. Is it an organization?

Group D: A Discord Fan Server 3,400 members who joined a server dedicated to a TV show. They share memes, debate plot points, and have volunteer moderators who enforce rules. There are no dues, no formal leadership, no stated goals. Is it an organization?

Group E: A Sunday Pickup Basketball Game 10 people who show up to the campus gym every Sunday morning to play basketball. No signup, no dues, no formal membership — just a recurring pattern. Is it an organization?

Group F: A Flash Mob 200 strangers who found each other online, coordinated to perform a choreographed dance in Union Station for 5 minutes, then dispersed and never interacted again. Is it an organization?

Group G: A Dormant Neighborhood Association Formally incorporated, has elected officers and bylaws, collects annual dues — but hasn’t held a meeting in 3 years and has no active members. Is it an organization?

Group H: The U.S. Federal Government 4 million employees, constitutional authority, explicit hierarchy, legal powers, and stated goals. Is it an organization?





Which ones were easiest to decide? Why?
Which were hardest? What made them hard?
What features seemed necessary for something to be an organization?
Did any of you change your mind after seeing what others marked?

Class Sessions
This course will be mostly discussion-based and application-centered. For the most part, you will engage with the content through doing readings before class, so that our time together can be used to go deeper — not to cover the basics.
Tuesday sessions are discussion-centric. Most of the session will be a conversation about that week’s readings, driven by your questions and ideas. I will use the discussion questions from your 3-2-1 assignments to guide us. This means I expect you to arrive on Tuesdays having done the reading.
Thursday sessions are more like a workshop. We will work through case studies in groups, applying the week’s concepts to real organizational scenarios. Some Thursdays will also be used for project work, peer feedback, or exams.

Academic Integrity
While I encourage collaboration, I expect that any work that you submit is your own. Basic guidelines for Purdue students are outlined here, but I expect you to be exemplary members of the academic community. Please get in touch if you have any questions or concerns.

AI Policy
Academic integrity also applies to AI. I am a technology optimist, and an AI optimist. I think AI can be an amazing tool for education and learning, but it can also be misused. The principle I expect you to follow is that you can’t (and shouldn’t) use AI as a shortcut (a tool that gives you answers). Instead, I completely support you using it as a scaffold (a tool that helps you think harder).
Specifically:

Write your own work. Don’t have AI write your reflections, essays, discussion questions, or final project prose. You can use AI to help you brainstorm, or to give you feedback on your writing, but you should be the one doing the writing.
Use AI to understand topics, readings, and concepts. Have AI explain a confusing passage, ask it to define terms, treat it like a patient tutor.
Disclose substantive AI use. I expect you to be transparent about the ways that you use AI in the class.

Pick an organization you know well enough to write specifically about. Vague generalizations don’t make for good analysis.

Avoid organizations so small or thin that there’s nothing to analyze.
Past organizations are fine — a former job, a team you’ve left, a group that no longer exists.

title: Case Study: The Lodestar Launch Decision
text:
Background
Lodestar Electric is a mid-sized electric vehicle manufacturer preparing to launch its first mass-market model, the Lodestar S. The launch has been in development for three years and is scheduled for eight weeks from now. Two thousand dealerships have pre-sold 18,000 units. The CEO has already appeared on the cover of Forbes with the headline “America’s EV Moment.”
One week before the final go/no-go decision meeting, the lead battery engineer, Daria Chen, submits an internal report flagging a thermal management issue. Under sustained high-speed driving in temperatures above 95°F, the battery cooling system may underperform, causing reduced range and, in rare cases, a risk of thermal runaway (battery fire). Her report estimates the probability of thermal runaway at approximately 1 in 4,000 vehicles under worst-case conditions.

title: Case Study: The Lodestar Launch Decision
text:
What Happened in the Meeting
The go/no-go meeting includes the CEO, CFO, VP of Engineering, VP of Marketing, General Counsel, and Daria Chen. Here is a summary of what each person said:

CEO: “We’ve spent $340 million getting here. Our competitors are six months behind us. Missing this launch window costs us everything. Daria, how confident are you in that 1-in-4,000 figure?”
CFO: “A recall post-launch would be catastrophic financially. But delaying also has massive costs. I’d want to see the data independently verified before we decide.”
VP of Engineering: “Every vehicle has edge-case risks. We exceeded all current federal safety standards. I think we’re fine.”
VP of Marketing: “If we delay now, the press narrative becomes ‘Lodestar can’t deliver.’ We can issue a software update post-launch to manage the thermal curve.”
General Counsel: “Federal standards are met. As long as we document that we reviewed the report, our liability exposure is limited.”
Daria Chen: “I want to be clear: I’m not saying don’t launch. I’m saying we need four more weeks to redesign the cooling loop. The fix is straightforward. The risk is low but it’s real.”

The CEO called for a show of hands. Everyone except Daria voted to launch on schedule.

title: Case Study: The Lodestar Launch Decision
text:
Group Tasks
Each group will analyze the case through one assigned decision-making model, then share findings with the class.


Group 1: The Rational Model
The rational model assumes decision-makers have complete information, evaluate all alternatives, and choose the option that maximizes outcomes.

In what ways did the Lodestar meeting follow the rational model?
In what ways did it fail to follow it? What information was missing, ignored, or not sought?
If the team had followed a fully rational process, what would the decision-making procedure have looked like — and would it have changed the outcome?




Group 2: Bounded Rationality
Herbert Simon argued that real decision-makers satisfice — they look for a “good enough” solution rather than the optimal one, because their information and cognitive capacity are limited.

What cognitive shortcuts or “satisficing” moves do you see in the meeting? Who was settling for “good enough,” and on what basis?
What information did participants use as a mental shortcut to avoid deeper analysis?
How did time pressure and sunk costs (“we’ve spent $340 million”) shape the decision? Is this rational, boundedly rational, or something else?




Group 3: Groupthink
Irving Janis identified groupthink as a pattern where the pressure to reach consensus overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives. Classic symptoms include: illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalization, self-censorship, illusion of unanimity, and pressure on dissenters.

Which groupthink symptoms appear in this meeting? Find specific evidence in the dialogue.
What communication dynamics silenced or minimized Daria Chen’s concern?
What specific procedural change — in how the meeting was structured or how voices were solicited — might have produced a different outcome?




Group 4: The Garbage Can Model
The garbage can model describes organizations as “organized anarchies” where problems, solutions, participants, and choice opportunities flow independently and connect somewhat randomly.

What different “problems” and “solutions” were floating around in this meeting, and did they actually match each other?
Is the go/no-go decision actually about the thermal issue — or are other problems (financial pressure, competitive timing, reputation) being channeled into this decision?
Who were the key participants, and how did their presence or absence shape what got decided?

title: Case Study: The Lodestar Launch Decision
text:
Whole-Class Discussion
After groups share out, we’ll discuss together:

Which model best explains what happened at Lodestar?
Are these models competing explanations, or can they all be true at the same time?
What does this case reveal about the role of communication — not just information — in organizational decision-making?

title: Group C: Homes for All Coalition
text: See the full activity overview for the questions your group should work through.

title: Group C: Homes for All Coalition
text:
Your Organization
Homes for All Coalition is a housing justice organization based in Indianapolis that works to prevent displacement, fight discriminatory housing practices, and expand access to affordable housing. Founded in 2011, it has a staff of 11 (6 full-time, 5 part-time), an annual budget of about $900,000, and an active membership base of roughly 600 people — mostly renters and low-income homeowners in neighborhoods facing rapid gentrification.
The organization does several kinds of work simultaneously: direct services (helping tenants navigate eviction proceedings), policy advocacy (lobbying city council and the state legislature), community organizing (building power among affected residents), and public communications (media outreach, social media, storytelling).
Internally, the organization tries to practice what it preaches. Decision-making is intentionally participatory: staff and member leaders share power through a governance structure that gives members a meaningful voice in organizational direction. This slows things down sometimes, but it also means that there are active attempts to listen to people most affected by housing policy when setting the agenda.
The coalition is part of a national network of similar organizations, which means regular communication with allied groups in other cities, shared strategy, and sometimes shared campaigns. Locally, they work in coalition with tenant unions, immigrant rights groups, faith communities, and labor unions — relationships that require constant maintenance and negotiation.
Funding comes from a mix of foundation grants, individual donors, and government contracts. Each comes with strings: foundations want measurable outcomes, government contracts restrict political activity, and individual donors have varying levels of engagement and expectation.

Work through the discussion questions with your group.
